source.title: Blockwise Adaptivity: Faster Training and Better Generalization in Deep Learning

record.tranche_reason: Compares coordinate-wise adaptive Adam with Nesterov’s accelerated gradient and tests blockwise adaptivity using held-out performance and training–test gaps; this is a conceptual test of the adaptive-optimizer generalization version.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out errors/perplexities for Adam, NAG, and BAGM variants, plus textual comparisons of their training, testing, and generalization-error curves. No random-label, width, convolution-versus-fully-connected, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example-removal experiments are reported.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares Adam with stochastic Nesterov momentum on image classification and with a zero-momentum NAG configuration on word-level language modeling. These held-out comparisons test V4, although momentum is also tuned and Adam's epsilon is fixed at 10^-3. The study is not an original source for V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate as an account of the authors' conclusion: they argue that blockwise adaptivity can accelerate convergence and lower generalization error, supported by theory and experiments. It should not imply every BAGM variant beats both baselines: on WikiText-2 only BAGM-B.2 beats Adam, and ImageNet top-5 results also vary by block scheme.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes blockwise adaptive gradient methods and compares them with Adam and NAG; it does not reproduce the original optimizer comparisons. Epsilon is set to 10−3 for adaptive methods, and selected hyperparameters are tuned using validation data.
record.method_sensitivity: Adam’s relative held-out result varies by model, dataset, and metric. The authors use epsilon 10−3 for adaptive methods; they state that larger epsilon reduces adaptivity and improves generalization. CIFAR-10 and ImageNet include weight decay and augmentation, while ImageNet also uses label smoothing and mixup.

fits_no_version.finding: BAGM variants improve CIFAR-10 and ImageNet top-1 performance over Adam; language and ImageNet top-5 rankings depend on block construction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Blockwise adaptivity can improve held-out performance over coordinate-wise Adam, depending on workload and block construction.

fits_no_version.finding: BAGM-B.1 has smaller training–test error gaps than Adam on both CIFAR-10 ResNets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Parameter-block adaptivity can reduce training–test error gaps relative to coordinate-wise adaptivity.

record.problems: The study says grid search over all hyperparameters was too computationally expensive and tunes only the most important ones. Results are averaged over 5 repetitions for CIFAR-10 curves and 3 for WikiText-2 perplexities, but the tables give no uncertainty estimates. ImageNet evaluation uses the validation set because test labels are unavailable.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported table results were omitted. Figure-only values were not reconstructed; the textual generalization-error comparisons are recorded in R30–R31 without numeric values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width dependence beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

A protocol tuning only learning rates and schedules; systematic comparison of limited versus broader tuning; epsilon intervention; decoupled weight decay; Adam-to-SGD switching; and a recorded comparison establishing worse held-out performance despite equal or better training performance.
Batch-size interventions under fixed epoch budgets and remedies for large-batch penalties.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removal of highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: NAG is a stochastic momentum baseline on images; the record's assertion that no SGD or momentum-SGD comparison exists is misleading. Momentum is tuned in addition to learning rate, and epsilon is fixed at 10^-3 without an epsilon sweep. The authors' explanation that larger epsilon improves Adam is therefore not an independently measured epsilon effect here. Small numerical differences lack reported uncertainty; no pooled verdict across models or metrics is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test-error trends.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.

No SGD or momentum-SGD comparison; tests Adam against NAG and blockwise adaptive variants. The optimizer comparison uses the authors’ selected tuning setup and does not test broader tuning, Adam-to-SGD switching, or decoupled weight decay.
No batch-size sweep or fixed-epoch comparison.
No dropout or weight-decay intervention comparison.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.

relation.reason: Its own Adam–NAG comparisons measure held-out image error and language-model perplexity relevant to V4.

tranche.reason: The study compares held-out performance of Adam and NAG using its own training and tuning recipes, addressing the optimizer-generalization question through a different method.

source_check.notes: The study fixes epsilon at 10^-3 and does not isolate the causal effect of broader tuning; numerical reversals should retain the uncertainty caveat. The authors' conclusion is broadly faithful, but individual BAGM variants do not uniformly beat both baselines.

statements.correction: ResNet56/CIFAR-10 test error: Adam 6.64%, NAG 6.91%; epsilon fixed at 10^-3 for adaptive methods; initial learning rate and momentum selected by validation grid search; no within-study comparison isolating the effect of expanding tuning; consistent with V4's broader-tuning clause.
statements.problem: The ResNet56 numbers are correct, but epsilon was fixed rather than searched. Calling this a challenge to V4 overlooks its explicit allowance for reversals under broader tuning.
